title: Sh-B-R
hookLine: shever, a break; mashber, a birthstool (Isaiah 37:3): breaking can bring birth

lines: THE PIECES WENT IN THE ARK.
cards: Stone tablets, carried down a mountain. Moses comes near the camp, sees the golden calf and the dancing, and in the King James words, "he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount."
Later he carves a second set and carries them up again. The Talmud adds a detail the Torah doesn't spell out: the broken pieces weren't swept away.
The rabbis teach that the whole tablets and the broken tablets were both placed in the ark, and carried together.

teach.b: Sh-B-R. Shin, bet, resh. Shever: a break, a fracture.
First, the heart. A psalm says, "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart." The Hebrew is nishberei lev, the broken of heart, from this root.
The verse doesn't say near the whole. It says near the broken. Second, a surprise.

A word from these same letters, mashber, turns up in Isaiah, when King Hezekiah sends a desperate message to the prophet: "for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth."
Where the King James says the birth, the Hebrew has mashber, which readers understand as the birthstool, where a woman in labor sat. Hezekiah uses it for a crisis that has stalled.
So one root holds two things: the break and the birth. Third, back to the ark.
The Talmud draws a lesson about people from it: honor an elder who has forgotten their learning through no fault of their own, because the broken tablets lay in the ark too.
Broken still belongs in the holiest place. Fourth, a careful word.
The tradition doesn't say every break is secretly good, or that pain is a present. Hezekiah's line is a cry: there is not strength to bring forth. The root simply won't let a break be only an ending.
It keeps a birthstool in the same letters.

how: Jewish teaching returns to the broken tablets kept in the ark beside the whole ones (Berakhot 8b) and to the psalm's promise that God is near the broken of heart; the Hebrew mashber, a birthstool in Isaiah 37:3, shares the root of shever, a break.

o: the Hebrew root of a shepherd and his flock
the Hebrew root of anger that boils over
the Hebrew root of a break, and the birthstool

p: kept in the ark beside the whole

s: the broken tablets were thrown away
the Talmud teaches they were placed in the ark beside the whole ones.
Hezekiah's mashber line is a cry of crisis
the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth.
the root teaches that every break is secretly good
it doesn't. it keeps break and birth in one root, and lets the cry stand.

games.q: you're Moses, coming down the mountain with the tablets, and you see the golden calf. what happens to the tablets?
o: you hide them until the people turn back.
you break them at the foot of the mountain.
games.why: "he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount." the Talmud adds that the pieces were kept, in the ark.

practice: Bring to mind something that cracked, a plan, a friendship, a body that stopped doing what it used to, a medium one, not the hardest, and hold it for a few breaths without trying to fix it.
Then ask gently whether anything began there; if nothing comes, that's an honest answer too, since the broken tablets were kept anyway.
If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.
And if a break ever feels too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Sh-B-R. Shin, bet, resh: shever, a break, and mashber, the birthstool. The tablets, the heart, the cry. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a break, a fracture, from shin, bet, resh; mashber, the birthstool, shares the letters.

carryVoice: Your line: breaking can birth. Can, not must; the broken pieces were kept either way. Take care of yourself.
